enrichment.short_title: Lady Archer's breach of confidence claim against former personal assistant
key_facts: Lady Archer employed Jane Williams as personal assistant from 1988 until dismissal in November 2001 after she refused to sign a confidentiality agreement.
Following termination, Williams disclosed confidential information to press intermediaries; a 13-page fax to News of the World was used in a Sunday Mirror article about cosmetic surgery.
Williams maintained working Filofax diaries recording the claimant's appointments; the parties disputed ownership.
Williams sought to publish details of home life, expenditure and diary-derived information; the claimant sought injunction, damages and delivery up.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial of claim for breach of confidence following without-notice and inter partes interim injunctions.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for the claimant: working diaries ordered delivered up; injunction granted (subject to drafting on paragraph 1(e)); £2,500 general damages awarded; defendant ordered to pay costs; charging order made for damages; interim costs order refused.
enrichment.ratio: A long-serving personal assistant owed continuing contractual and equitable duties of confidence after employment; where proposed disclosures concerned private medical, financial and domestic matters of limited public interest, Article 8 outweighed the defendant's Article 10 defence under section 12 of the Human Rights Act 1998; the employer-owned working diaries remained the claimant's property.
legal_issues: Whether working diaries maintained by the PA were the claimant's property
Scope of contractual and equitable duties of confidence after termination of employment
Whether section 12 HRA 1998 and Article 10 permitted publication of the proposed disclosures
Liability and quantum for past breach of confidence including the Sunday Mirror leak
Costs, interim costs, wasted costs and charging order applications

enrichment.short_title: Lambeth housing allocation reassessment after unlawful Group D scheme
key_facts: In July 2002 the Court of Appeal held Lambeth's July 2000 housing allocation scheme unlawful, particularly Group D, and ordered reassessment of claimants' applications by 31 August 2002.
Applicant Lindsay maintained entitlement to reassessment; co-claimant A was reassessed and took no further part.
Lambeth sought extension citing practical difficulties implementing a new lawful policy until February 2004.
Before the court could explore justification, the parties reached agreed terms on compliance with paragraph 3 of the earlier order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Further hearing before Pill and Judge LJ on Lambeth's application for extension of time under liberty to apply following earlier Court of Appeal decision.
enrichment.outcome: No further order made; parties' settlement on reassessment accepted; applicant awarded costs; Sullivan J's declaration of illegality remained undisturbed.
enrichment.ratio: Where parties settle implementation of a reassessment order, the court need not adjudicate further on extension arguments; a consent arrangement on reassessment does not prevent other applicants challenging the council's continued use of an unlawful allocation scheme.
legal_issues: Whether Lambeth should be granted further time to implement a lawful housing allocation scheme
Whether Lindsay remained entitled to individual reassessment under the earlier order
Effect of the parties' settlement on pending challenges by other applicants

enrichment.short_title: Judicial review of Breckland Farmland SSSI confirmation for stone-curlew

statutes_considered.title: Countryside and Rights of Way Act 2000

key_facts: English Nature confirmed notification of Breckland Farmland SSSI covering over 13,335 hectares for its internationally important stone-curlew population.
Claimants challenged only the confirmation decision, not the notification or listed operations likely to damage (OLDs).
The site supported about 102 pairs in 1999 (44% of the GB population) and fell within a proposed Breckland SPA.
Claimants argued English Nature acted irrationally, exceeded jurisdiction, wrongly deferred to SPA policy, and breached Article 1 Protocol 1 ECHR by preferring SSSI over SPA/voluntary measures.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of English Nature's section 28(5) confirmation decision.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where English Nature continues to hold the expert opinion that land is of special interest, section 28 affords no discretion to refuse confirmation because alternative protection mechanisms such as SPA classification or voluntary agreements would be less onerous; alleged DETR pressure did not vitiate a decision properly taken on statutory criteria; Article 1 challenge to the confirmation decision itself was misconceived.
legal_issues: Construction of section 28 notification and confirmation duties
Whether English Nature could lawfully decline confirmation because SPA or voluntary protection was preferable
Whether designation of extensive arable land for mobile nesting stone-curlews was within jurisdiction
Whether confirmation was taken for irrelevant reasons linked to SPA policy
Article 1 Protocol 1 proportionality of SSSI confirmation

enrichment.short_title: Solicitor negligence appeal on permission to re-amend particulars of damage
key_facts: Gibrail and Salt personally underwrote Incomechance Ltd's purchase of shares in Nightingale Signs Ltd; after cash-flow failure they were sued to judgment and became bankrupt.
Former solicitors Birchall Blackburn sued Gibrail for fees; he obtained assignment from his trustee of rights relating to the underlying claims.
Judge Kershaw refused permission to re-amend defence and counterclaim to schedule eight heads of consequential loss, citing possible limitation and assignment issues.
Sedley LJ held the judge failed to address whether new damage particulars amplified an existing pleaded wrong or amounted to a new claim under CPR 17.4.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Restored application for permission to appeal; appeal heard immediately upon grant.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted; appeal allowed in part; refusal to re-amend set aside; limited permission to amend particulars of damage granted.
enrichment.ratio: Where a litigant in person seeks to particularise damage for an already pleaded breach of retainer, the court must ask whether the amendment adds a new claim or merely quantifies injury arising from substantially the same facts; if the latter, CPR 17.4 may permit amendment despite expiry of limitation, but many speculative heads of consequential loss in a solicitor-negligence claim are not recoverable.
legal_issues: Whether refusal to permit re-amendment of counterclaim particulars was flawed for failing to apply CPR 17.4
Whether proposed heads of damage were time-barred new claims or amplification of existing claims
Whether assigned causes of action covered company losses pursued in Gibrail's name
Which scheduled heads of damage were legally recoverable in professional negligence

enrichment.short_title: Arbitrator's power to order specific performance of lease refurbishment works
key_facts: Telia leased property from Hilcourt under an August 2000 agreement requiring commencement of substantial refurbishment works within ten working days of lease completion.
Telia commenced works late and allegedly failed to complete them; Hilcourt sought mandatory relief in arbitration.
The arbitrator held he had jurisdiction because the building obligation in clause 4.1 was separable and not a contract relating to land within section 48(5)(b).
Telia appealed the second interim award on jurisdiction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal on preliminary issue from arbitrator's second interim award under section 67 Arbitration Act 1996.
enrichment.ratio: Section 48(5)(b) excludes from an arbitrator's default specific-performance power only contracts for the creation or transfer of an interest in land; where relief sought concerns a separable post-grant obligation to carry out building works, the restriction does not apply even though the obligation formed part of the consideration for the lease.
legal_issues: Whether Hilcourt's claim was in substance specific performance rather than a mandatory injunction
Whether the lease agreement remained a contract relating to land after the lease was granted
Whether section 48(5)(b) applies to the whole agreement or only the obligation sought to be enforced
Proper construction of 'contract relating to land' in section 48(5)(b)

enrichment.short_title: Coroner must resume inquest where Article 2 arguable after estate stabbing
key_facts: Troy Hurst was fatally stabbed on 25 May 2000 by neighbour Albert Reid on a Barnet council estate; Reid was convicted of manslaughter.
The inquest was adjourned under section 16(1); after conviction the coroner refused twice to resume it under section 16(3).
Extensive police and housing records showed Reid's long history of violence, threats, mental health concerns and imminent possession proceedings; Troy Hurst was a witness.
On the fatal evening police responded to calls but did not fully search Reid's home for weapons or adequately protect the Hurst family.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review with leave of Hooper J to quash the coroner's refusal to resume an adjourned inquest.
enrichment.outcome: Coroner's decisions quashed; coroner ordered to resume the inquest; claimant's costs ordered against coroner; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Article 2's investigative duty can apply to a coroner's post-HRA decision even where the death occurred before the Human Rights Act came into force; a coroner must resume an inquest where there is sufficient evidence of an arguable Osman breach by public authorities, and the criminal trial did not substitute for that inquiry.
legal_issues: Whether Article 2 applied to the coroner's 2002-2003 decisions despite the 2000 death predating the HRA
Whether there was sufficient cause under section 16(3) to resume the inquest
Whether the criminal trial satisfied Article 2 investigative requirements
Whether evidence showed an arguable real and immediate risk known to police and/or the housing authority

enrichment.short_title: Part 20 costs after discontinued third party claim and failed fourth party claim
key_facts: Kingstons sued Francis brothers for roadway completion; the claim against them was held hopeless because Moody's covenant had been assigned.
Francis brothers issued third party proceedings against Moody and the McLays; Moody issued fourth party proceedings against the McLays for indemnity.
Francis brothers discontinued the third party claim against McLays before trial; fourth party claim against McLays failed at first instance but succeeded on appeal.
Judge Tibber made no order as to Part 20 costs between Francis brothers, Moody and McLays.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Restored cross-appeal against county court judge's no-order costs decision in Part 20 proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Cross-appeal dismissed; no order as to costs upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Where Part 20 claims involve an indirect indemnity chain and one route succeeded while a direct discontinued claim failed, a court may properly make no order as to costs to avoid circular recovery through successive indemnities and further assessment disputes.
legal_issues: Whether McLays were entitled to costs of the discontinued third party claim under CPR 38.6
Whether failure on the fourth party claim required McLays to pay Moody's costs
How to exercise discretion on costs where indemnity chains would recirculate any award

enrichment.short_title: Setting aside default damages judgment after alleged back pain non-attendance
key_facts: Thomson Directories sued Hutcheon and associated companies for unlicensed use of database material; all defendants submitted to an inquiry as to damages by consent in July 2001.
On 6 March 2003 Deputy Judge Steinfeld proceeded with the inquiry in Hutcheon's absence after rejecting an adjournment based on claimed chronic back pain.
Hutcheon obtained a medical certificate exempting him from work but not stating he could not attend court; he had driven from London to Liverpool that night.
Judgment was entered for about £1.3 million damages plus interest; Hutcheon applied under CPR 39.3 to set aside.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application to set aside judgment entered after non-attendance at inquiry as to damages.
enrichment.ratio: Under CPR 39.3(5) all three conditions must be satisfied to set aside a regular judgment for non-attendance; a defendant who decided not to attend before obtaining medical evidence, failed to act with reasonable celerity in issuing the application, and could not show a good reason for absence will not succeed.
legal_issues: Whether Hutcheon acted promptly within CPR 39.3(5)(a)
Whether there was a good reason for not attending the inquiry under CPR 39.3(5)(b)
Whether there was a reasonable prospect of success at trial under CPR 39.3(5)(c)
Effect of Lloyd J's timetable order on the setting-aside application

enrichment.short_title: Judicial review of section 106A approval to expand rival garden centre goods
key_facts: Greenholm Nurseries' 1991 planning permission and section 106 agreement restricted retail goods at a Congresbury nursery site under Local Plan Policy S5.

Competitor Cadbury Garden Centre challenged North Somerset Council's November 2002 in-principle approval to modify the section 106 obligation to add farm shop, seasonal, outdoor pursuits and other non-core goods.
An earlier March 2002 approval was quashed by consent; the council re-decided and again approved in principle subject to detailed list and floor area limits.
Officers consistently advised refusal because the proposed modifications would not serve the obligation's purpose equally well.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Planning and Regulatory Committee resolution of 6 November 2002 approving in principle a section 106A modification application.
enrichment.outcome: Resolution quashed; claim on range-of-goods application succeeded; separate glasshouse challenge abandoned with costs order against claimant.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 106A(6)(c) the authority must decide whether the planning obligation would serve its useful purpose equally well if modified as proposed; where the purpose includes securing compliance with countryside retail policy (Policy S5), approval of a wholesale expansion into general food and non-garden retail cannot rationally meet the 'equally well' test and members must apply that statutory test to the application as a whole.
legal_issues: Whether the November 2002 resolution was a reviewable decision or premature
Correct construction and application of section 106A(6)(c) 'equally well' test
Whether members failed to understand the statutory question
Whether comparison with neighbouring Cadbury Garden Centre was irrelevant
Whether the proposed modifications complied with Policy S5

enrichment.short_title: Discretion to extend time for homelessness review after intentional homelessness finding
key_facts: M.C., a vulnerable young woman with history of trauma and depression, lost her Lewisham flat in April 2000 after persistent rent arrears.
On 24 January 2001 Lewisham found her intentionally homeless for failing to pay rent and manage housing benefit claims.
She failed to request a section 202 review within 21 days; later psychiatric evidence linked her mental state to inability to manage affairs.
After repeated requests, the council refused on 25 October 2001 and again on 4 March 2002 to extend time for review.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against refusal of judicial review of Lewisham's refusal to extend time under section 202(3) Housing Act 1996.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; refusal to extend time upheld; Dr Browne's second report excluded.
enrichment.ratio: Section 202(3) confers a wide but principled discretion: delay and explanation for lateness are relevant, and it is not unlawful for a housing authority also to consider prospects of success of the underlying review; materiality of fresh evidence may properly be weighed as part of that assessment, and only one statutory application to extend time is envisaged though further extra-statutory reconsideration remains possible.
legal_issues: Proper approach to exercising discretion under section 202(3) to extend time for a homelessness review
Whether prospects of success on review is a relevant consideration
Whether the council's refusal was Wednesbury unreasonable
Whether Dr Browne's second report should be admitted
Whether repeated requests for review or extension lie outside the statutory scheme
